implementation_notes: Java has no inline keyword; the JIT decides at runtime based on profile data, and its rules are worth knowing because they explain most 'why is this slow'. The JIT inlines small methods, inlines a method on a hot path, and - critically - inlines a virtual call only at a monomorphic call site (one receiver type observed); at a bimorphic site it may still inline with a guard, and at a megamorphic site (three or more types) it stops inlining and uses a vtable dispatch. So the Java optimisation question is usually not 'should I inline' but 'can I make this call site monomorphic' - by using a concrete type, an instanceof guard, or by splitting the call site. Java 21's virtual threads do not change inlining. There is no source-level hint; the JDK's answer to 'I want this inlined' is to make the method small and the call site monomorphic.
idiom_name: JIT inlining (small methods, hot call sites, monomorphic virtual calls); no source-level inline keyword
pitfalls: There is no source-level inline hint in Java; making the callee small and the call site monomorphic is the lever.
A megamorphic call site (3+ receiver types) stops the JIT inlining regardless of how small the callee is - this is the single biggest cause of 'why did my optimisation not work'.
Inlining decisions depend on runtime profile data, so a method is inlined in production and not in a short unit test - measure under representative load.
Deeply recursive or very large methods exceed the inlining budget (MaxInlineSize/FreqInlineSize) and are not inlined regardless of hotness.
Interfaces defeat inlining the same way a megamorphic call does; a concrete receiver at the call site is the fix.
